title: Where the Cut Is
scopeNote: This keeps the schematic pathway that updates and the two field diagrams beside it. Both halves are needed: a defect without the pathway is a picture to memorise, and a pathway without the defect is anatomy without a consequence. The inference run backwards from a defect to the possible sites, macular sparing, and further sites along the pathway stay in the longer version.
summary: Break the visual pathway at one of five points and watch which parts of which eye's field go dark. Two of the sites produce the identical pattern, which is the point at which the forward exercise stops being a lookup table.
learningObjectives: Predict the field defect produced by damage at a given point on the visual pathway.
Explain why damage before the chiasm affects one eye and damage after it affects both.
Explain why a chiasm lesion removes the outer half of each eye's view rather than the same side of both.
Explain why damage further back can remove a quarter rather than a half.
Recognise that a field pattern narrows the possible sites without pinning one down.
interactionTypes: a schematic pathway redrawn with the break marked
two field circles shaded quadrant by quadrant
a named defect and a count of how much is gone
a guided case showing the one pattern that is not the same side in both eyes
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with the site chosen by a labelled radio group rather than by clicking the diagram. Selecting a site from the guided button moves the radio as well as the drawing, so the control and the figure never disagree. A lost quadrant is drawn as a solid dark wedge against a pale intact one, and the break is marked with a cross and a label as well as a colour. Each field circle is labelled with whose eye it is and with left and right of the person's view, so the orientation convention is on the figure rather than assumed. The description names the site, states in words which quadrants each eye has lost, and names the resulting defect, so nothing depends on reading the diagram. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
dataStatus: A schematic. No real patient, scan or perimetry result is described.
simulationNotes: Each field circle is drawn as the person sees the world, so the left of the circle is the left of their view. That convention is the easy thing to get wrong: fibres from the nasal retina cross at the chiasm, and nasal retina sees the temporal field, so the crossing fibres carry the outer side of each eye's view. Cutting the chiasm therefore removes the outer half of both fields rather than the same side of both, which is the only such pattern in the set. The optic tract and the primary visual cortex are given deliberately identical patterns, because a learner who notices that the mapping is many-to-one has understood something the forward exercise alone does not teach, and the readout says so rather than leaving it to be discovered.
readmeTopic: how the shape of a field defect locates the damage that caused it
